statement: Three of the eight corners of a cube are painted red. Two painted cubes count as the same if one can be turned to look exactly like the other. How many different painted cubes are there?

choices.misconception: I sorted the red corners into 'all on one face' or 'not all on one face', and missed that the second kind splits into two shapes.
I counted the triangle with an edge, a face diagonal and a long diagonal and its mirror image as different, but a turn takes one to the other.
I took the $\binom{8}{3} = 56$ choices and divided by 8, the number of corners.
I counted every choice of three corners, $\binom{8}{3}$, and forgot that turning the cube makes many of them the same.

hints: The three red corners form a triangle. What lengths can its sides have?

Any two corners of a cube are joined by an edge, a face diagonal or a long diagonal through the middle. Sort the red triangles by their three side types and check each type is one shape up to turning.
The possible triangles are: edge, edge, face diagonal (all on one face); three face diagonals; and edge, face diagonal, long diagonal. Check the counts add up to 56.

solutions.reliable: Two corners are joined by an edge (length 1), a face diagonal ($\sqrt{2}$) or a long diagonal ($\sqrt{3}$). Three red corners form a triangle of one of these types: (1) edge, edge, face diagonal, three corners of one face: $6 \times 4 = 24$ choices; (2) three face diagonals, an equilateral triangle cut off around one corner: 8 choices; (3) edge, face diagonal, long diagonal: the remaining $56 - 24 - 8 = 24$ choices. In types (1) and (3) only the 'do nothing' turn keeps such a triangle in place, so the cube's 24 turns make 24 different copies of one triangle, which is the whole type. In type (2) the 3 turns about a long diagonal keep the triangle in place, so the 24 turns make 8 copies, again the whole type. So there are 3 different cubes. The transferable idea: up to symmetry, classify by something turning cannot change, such as distances, then check each class is a single shape.

whyOnTest: Counting up to rotation means classifying by invariants such as distances; dividing the raw count by something is the tempting wrong shortcut.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
